performance-review.name: Performance Review
performance-review.summary: Analytical review of individual, team, or company performance grounded in metrics. Walks through results, key drivers, wins, challenges, and the adjustments that will shape the next period.

beats.name: Briefing
beats.description: Frame what this review covers: the period, the unit, the standard you're measuring against. One slide that lets the audience know exactly what they're being asked to evaluate.

beats.name: Results
beats.description: Lead with the headline result. On track, ahead, or behind, and by how much. Resist softening — clear numbers up front earn credibility for the analysis that follows.

beats.name: Key Metrics
beats.description: Walk through the pivotal indicators. One chart per metric, clear comparison period, target or benchmark visible on the same frame. Help the audience see the data the way you do.

beats.name: Team Performance
beats.description: Examine collective achievements and how the team contributed. Avoid generic praise; cite specific moves and the people behind them where the audience would expect it.

beats.name: Highlight
beats.description: Spotlight one standout contribution that defined the period. A landmark deal, a launch, a fix, a hire. One vivid example sticks longer than a list of accomplishments.

beats.name: Analysis
beats.description: Dig under the metrics. What drove the numbers, what held them back, what's signal versus noise. Analysis is where the audience learns whether you actually understand the system you're reporting on.

beats.name: Success
beats.description: Reinforce the past triumphs that show the system works. Briefly — the audience came for what's next, not a victory lap. Wins earn permission for the harder slides ahead.

beats.name: Challenges
beats.description: Name the obstacles encountered honestly. What didn't move, what regressed, what the team is still wrestling with. Understated challenges read as missed signal, not modesty.

beats.name: Adjustments
beats.description: Identify the changes you're making in response. New tactics, reallocations, sunsets. Each adjustment should map to a challenge above — adjustments without diagnosis feel arbitrary.

beats.name: Strategy Evolution
beats.description: Show how the strategy itself evolves heading into the next period. Refinements, sharpened bets, dropped initiatives. The audience should see continuity as well as change.

beats.name: Discussion
beats.description: Open the floor with two or three specific prompts. End the review actively — questions you want answered, decisions you want made — so the meeting yields more than the deck.

engineering-team.name: Engineering Team
engineering-team.summary: Practitioners building the system; they want depth, mechanism, and tradeoffs.
engineering-team.description: Engineers tune out generalities and tune in to specifics. Show benchmarks with conditions, architecture diagrams with constraints, and tradeoffs you actually considered. Internal jargon is fine — assume the room shares it. Leave room for questions; engineering audiences engage best when they can poke at the proposal.

inform.name: Inform
inform.summary: Give the audience clear context, facts, or status without asking for a decision.
inform.description: Use when the deck needs to make the audience aware of current state, background, or findings. Prioritize clarity, completeness, and accurate framing over persuasion.
inform.outcome: The audience understands the situation and can repeat the important facts.
successCriteria: Audience can summarize the key facts
Follow-up questions are about implications, not basic context

authoritative.name: Authoritative
authoritative.summary: Expert, declarative voice for category-defining and analyst-style decks.
authoritative.description: Adopt the perspective of someone who's seen the full landscape and is willing to call it. Use plain declaratives — strong claims with the receipts to back them. Step back from internal-only context and frame in terms the wider industry would recognize.
voiceCues: Use declarative sentences; trust the reader to follow.
Frame in industry-wide terms, not company-internal language.
Cite outside sources — analysts, benchmarks, public peers.
Take a position; avoid 'on the other hand' symmetry without a verdict.
avoid: Hedging ('we believe', 'in our view') unless deliberately contrasting.
First-person plural overload — speak for the work, not the team.
Tentative phrasing that softens strong claims.
samplePhrases: Agent latency is the bottleneck of the next AI cycle.
Three categories will absorb 80% of enterprise budget; we're built for the second.
The benchmarks are public; the gap holds across every comparable workload.

classic.name: Classic
classic.description: A timeless, clean, and versatile theme with balanced color contrasts and classic typography. Ideal for professional, readable presentations.

forest-green.name: Forest Green
forest-green.summary: Organic green palette for growth, health, and sustainability stories.
forest-green.description: A green and soft-neutral scheme for decks about growth, renewal, wellness, and environmental impact.

cool-horizon.name: Cool Horizon
cool-horizon.summary: Cool blue-green palette tuned for professional business decks.
cool-horizon.description: A balanced cool-toned scheme with deep navy, business blues, and teal accents. It works well across strategy, finance, and technical narratives.

segoe-ui.name: Segoe UI
segoe-ui.description: Segoe UI is a sans serif OPF font scheme for Latin presentations, using Segoe UI Semibold for headings with Segoe UI for body text.

tenorite.name: Tenorite
tenorite.description: Tenorite is a sans serif OPF font scheme for Latin presentations, using Tenorite Display for headings with Tenorite for body text.

cover.name: Cover
cover.summary: The opening slide: title, subtitle and an optional picture.
cover.description: Open a presentation with its subject and a short introduction. Add a picture when it helps establish the context.

text.name: Text
text.summary: Prose. Several blocks sit side by side when short and stack when long.
text.description: Explain one idea in continuous prose. Use paragraphs or flowing blocks for detail that needs to be read in sequence.

chart.name: Chart
chart.summary: One to six charts, with an optional note.
chart.description: Give a chart enough space to show its evidence. Use the title to state the conclusion and labels to explain the measures.

list.name: List
list.summary: Bulleted or numbered points; one long list flows into columns.
list.description: Present several related points in a clear sequence. Use bullets for independent points or numbered items for an ordered list.
